{"id": "17:86/q10", "question": "What setting or incident is associated with this warning?", "turns_on": "The notes give different circumstances for invoking the warning: ancestral religion, delay over spirit, or the Yemen delegation's encounter.", "positions": [{"id": "17:86/q10/p1", "position": "It warned Muhammad after he was invited to his forefathers' religion.", "reasons": "Muqātil says God could take the Qurʾān away and no protector could prevent Him."}, {"id": "17:86/q10/p2", "position": "It followed the delayed answer about spirit and addressed the Prophet's distress and need for decorum.", "reasons": "The al-Taḥrīr explanation reported by Abū Ḥayyān says the verse consoled and reassured Muhammad; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it rebukes his promise to answer the next day and teaches submission to God's choice of what to reveal or withhold."}, {"id": "17:86/q10/p3", "position": "After a Yemen delegation tested his prophethood, the Prophet recited the warning while expressing fear of straying.", "reasons": "The report in al-Durr has the delegation pose a riddle and test him through speaking pebbles; they hear his recitation and weep, and he describes his assigned path as razor edged before citing this verse."}]}
{"id": "17:86/q11", "question": "What do reports say about the future lifting of the Qurʾān?", "turns_on": "The reports vary in agent and setting (red wind from Syria, Gabriel, or no agent), timing and destination, cause, and what remains afterward; al-Dimashqī contests sudden extraction by citing a Prophetic statement about knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "17:86/q11/p1", "position": "It will be withdrawn overnight from hearts and written copies, leaving no verse accessible.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd is reported by al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Durr, and Study Quran; al-Thaʿlabī adds that trust disappears first, prayer and praying people last, and people are left like beasts. Al-Durr gives shorter variants emphasizing every codex, every inner memory, or no verse on earth or in a Muslim's body; a Prophetic report commands adherence to the Book after his departure. Shamr ibn ʿAṭiya says night worshippers cannot recite from memory or copies and gather to tell each other of the loss. The Prophet, as reported through Ḥudhayfa and Abū Hurayra, says no verse remains on earth. Ibn Masʿūd in Study Quran similarly frames the loss between trust and prayer."}, {"id": "17:86/q11/p2", "position": "A red wind from Syria will erase every verse from codices and hearts at the end of time.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd gives the red wind's place of origin in reports in al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr; al-Ṭabarī says even a collector of the Qurʾān loses it. Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites the same report and this verse to establish that the event is possible."}, {"id": "17:86/q11/p3", "position": "Gabriel will take the Qurʾān from people's breasts and homes in one night.", "reasons": "The report in Ibn al-Jawzī says people wake unable to recite or even sense a verse; the named agent here is Gabriel."}, {"id": "17:86/q11/p4", "position": "Reports of sudden Qurʾān extraction are unsound or may concern other knowledge; Qurʾān removal would come last.", "reasons": "Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī, reported by Ibn al-Jawzī, invokes the Prophet's statement that knowledge is not seized by sudden extraction; even sound chains for Ibn Masʿūd's report could refer to knowledge other than Qurʾān."}, {"id": "17:86/q11/p5", "position": "At the end of time the Qurʾān is lifted because people recite without obeying it.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr says this in al-Thaʿlabī. In al-Durr, he adds that it sounds like bees around the Throne and protests that it was recited but not acted on. Ibn ʿUmar in Study Quran says it returns to its place of descent and complains for the same reason before the Hour."}, {"id": "17:86/q11/p6", "position": "The Qurʾān is lifted when people abandon it for other books.", "reasons": "Al-Layth ibn Saʿd gives that cause in al-Durr."}, {"id": "17:86/q11/p7", "position": "The Book is lifted to heaven with the Torah, Gospel, and Psalms.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra says this in al-Durr and adds that people will not know what they do in prayer."}, {"id": "17:86/q11/p8", "position": "The Qurʾān will be lifted from earth before the Hour, along with remembrance.", "reasons": "An Abū Hurayra Prophetic report says a time comes when it is sent for and lifted; Jābir reports the Prophet saying the Hour awaits the lifting of remembrance and Qurʾān."}, {"id": "17:86/q11/p9", "position": "After overnight withdrawal, those favored by God will still retain the testimony of faith.", "reasons": "The Prophet says 'There is no god but God' remains in the heart when other written material is removed, in al-Thaʿlabī. Another Prophetic report in al-Durr says Islam wears away like a garment, leaving elderly people who repeat the testimony without knowledge of prayer, fasting, or rites. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn ʿUmar transmit a warning against writing other books with God's Book and the same exception for the testimony. Ḥudhayfa says Qurʾān loses its sweetness and hearts forget the rites when it is removed overnight."}, {"id": "17:86/q11/p10", "position": "People should recite and perform pilgrimage before the Qurʾān is withdrawn, since afterward they forget and revert to older customs or poetry.", "reasons": "A report from ʿAbd Allāh in al-Thaʿlabī urges abundant pilgrimage and recitation before overnight removal and says people forget the testimony and follow pre-Islamic customs. Ibn Masʿūd in al-Durr urges recitation before night lifting and says people forget knowledge and turn to poetry."}]}
{"id": "17:86/q12", "question": "What is the warning's teaching and purpose?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize different implications of the same threat: God's control, gratitude for a favor, restraint in questioning, and dependence on revelation for ethics.", "positions": [{"id": "17:86/q12/p1", "position": "Revelation is wholly God's gift and under His control; its recipients should depend on His mercy and submit to what He discloses.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says God can take back what He gave and links it to humanity's little knowledge; al-Ṭabrisī says God mercifully supplies what the Prophet needs but withholds unneeded details even when people think them necessary. Ibn ʿAṭiyya applies it to the Prophet's next-day promise. Abū Ḥayyān says the power to reveal entails the power to withdraw, though God did not withdraw it. Islāḥī says the Prophet can neither acquire, refuse, nor retain revelation at will. Kur'an Yolu says all knowledge comes from God, no other power can protect, restore, or replace it; its example of earlier scriptures illustrates this dependence."}, {"id": "17:86/q12/p2", "position": "It recalls a great favor and calls for gratitude and humility about knowledge.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr calls the revealed Qurʾān a great favor and joins it to 17:88: even cooperating humans and jinn cannot produce its like because created speech cannot match the Creator. Al-Nasafī says the gift consoles the Prophet through argumentative questioning. Ibn ʿĀshūr connects Qurʾānic healing and mercy to gratitude rather than conceit; the explicit threat indirectly declares favor, as the next verse clarifies, and admonishes scholars too. Study Quran says the warning and mercy exception express the favor of revealing and preserving Qurʾān in hearts and writing, and cites the pairing of mercy and bounty at 2:64, 4:83, 4:113, 4:175, 24:10, 24:14, and 24:20."}, {"id": "17:86/q12/p3", "position": "It cautions against improper questions about withheld knowledge.", "reasons": "Abū Sahl says it threatens removal of what people do possess if they press for knowledge not granted, such as the spirit or Hour. The al-Taḥrīr explanation says it teaches the Prophet decorum after delayed disclosure about spirit."}, {"id": "17:86/q12/p4", "position": "It shows that only revelation supplies an absolute ethical guide.", "reasons": "Asad says, if it were removed, no alternative guide could perform its role."}]}
{"id": "17:86/q13", "question": "How does the verse connect with the surrounding verses?", "turns_on": "The sources attach the warning to different adjacent themes: little knowledge and spirit, divine mercy after the warning, or the Qurʾān's inimitability.", "positions": [{"id": "17:86/q13/p1", "position": "It follows 17:85's statement that people were given little knowledge: God could withdraw even that gift.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Biqāʿī, and Study Quran make this link. Al-Wāḥidī also reports a reading in which the preceding address includes the Prophet and believers, whose knowledge of spirit was withheld; the threat to withdraw revelation supports it. Al-Ṭabrisī says the erasure reading suggests the spirit question concerned Qurʾān, whereas al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the warning fits other readings of spirit too."}, {"id": "17:86/q13/p2", "position": "It follows accounts of revelation as healing, mercy, and a force that steadied the Prophet, and points toward mercy's preservation of it.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī recalls both healing and the thwarted effort to divert the Prophet; al-Biqāʿī mentions attempts to alter revelation and expel the Messenger. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the next verse makes the implied favor explicit. Study Quran says mercy may mean God declines to remove the Qurʾān or restores it afterward. Elmalılı says the Lord who revealed it preserves it and sustains Muhammad through special grace intended to spread universal mercy; al-Ṭabrisī says God gives necessary revelation while withholding needless detail."}, {"id": "17:86/q13/p3", "position": "The next challenge shows that the Qurʾān is a unique divine gift beyond human and jinn imitation.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says no coalition of humans and jinn can produce its like, since created speech cannot match the Creator."}]}

": [{"id": "17:86/q14/p1", "position": "Revelation can be effaced in annihilation or veiled after disclosure as spiritual states change; only merciful manifestation sustains revelation and the self.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says no agent can restore revelation if veiled. A direct manifestation of the divine essence would leave neither revelation nor the Prophet's self, while manifestation through mercy brings both into being and majesty can veil revelation and knowledge."}]}
{"id": "17:87/q01", "question": "How is the mercy exception construed against the preceding warning?", "turns_on": "Whether mercy is outside the preceding class, belongs among possible advocates, gives the purpose or verbal force of the clause, or supplies an omitted statement; the connected reading is challenged over the sense of advocate and what counts as the further favor.", "positions": [{"id": "17:87/q01/p1", "position": "It is a disconnected exception: God's mercy instead prevents the loss of revelation or keeps it with the Prophet.", "reasons": "Al-Farra compares the exception in 12:68; al-Zajjaj and al-Wahidi's Abu Ishaq say God fixed revelation in the Prophet's and believers' hearts. Al-Nahhas also allows mercy to restore lost knowledge. Ibn Atiyya stresses that mercy is outside the preceding category and disputes the view attributed to Ibn Khuwayz Mindad that the Qur'an lacks disconnected exceptions. Al-Tabrisi relates it to the preceding statement. Al-Samin says Basrans supply lakin and Kufans bal. Al-Kashf, preferred by al-Alusi, takes it to correct the claim that no advocate could restore the Qur'an; al-Alusi says this reading makes preservation a further favor after revelation. Ibn Ashur calls it a qualification of a hypothetical removal. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi, and al-Nasafi also report a connected alternative."}, {"id": "17:87/q01/p2", "position": "It is connected to the missing guardian or advocate: divine mercy itself can secure the Qur'an's return.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari includes mercy among the possible protectors against loss. Al-Samin likewise takes it under guardian. Al-Bursevi prefers a personified mercy advocating restoration. Al-Alusi reports this parse but says making mercy an advocate strains the expression; he also says it obscures the additional favor of preservation. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi, and al-Nasafi offer restoration as an alternative."}, {"id": "17:87/q01/p3", "position": "Mercy is an accusative purpose complement: God preserved revelation for mercy.", "reasons": "Al-Kawwashi supplies this purpose construction in al-Bursevi; Abu al-Baqa supplies it in al-Alusi."}, {"id": "17:87/q01/p4", "position": "Mercy is an accusative verbal noun or absolute object: God showed mercy.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi calls rahmatan a verbal noun; Abu al-Baqa, as reported by al-Alusi, calls it an absolute object."}, {"id": "17:87/q01/p5", "position": "An implicit clause says that revelation was sent, received, or retained only by the Lord's mercy.", "reasons": "Yahya ibn Sallam supplies God's sending of the Qur'an to the Prophet. Al-Tabatabai supplies the Prophet's receiving and retaining the Spirit."}]}
{"id": "17:87/q02", "question": "What does the Lord's mercy accomplish here?", "turns_on": "Whether mercy primarily prevents loss, restores a loss, grants revelation initially, or, in al-Qashani's inward account, sustains existence and revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "17:87/q02/p1", "position": "It keeps the Qur'an or its knowledge with the Prophet and believers, preventing its threatened erasure.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls the Qur'an a special grant; al-Zajjaj, al-Wahidi's Abu Ishaq, al-Wahidi al-Wajiz, and al-Tabrisi stress its establishment in hearts. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, al-Bursevi's Kashifi, al-Alusi, and Ibn Ashur connect preservation to favor. Al-Kashshaf and al-Razi add that scholars should thank God for retained knowledge. Ibn Ashur cites 15:9; Kur'an Yolu adds transmission without corruption, while Study Quran says preservation is in hearts and writing and cites 2:64, 4:83, 4:113, 4:175, 24:10, 24:14, and 24:20 for the pairing of mercy and bounty. Elmalili calls this special grace the basis for spreading universal mercy."}, {"id": "17:87/q02/p2", "position": "It can restore revelation or knowledge after God takes it away.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas allows restored knowledge even while calling the exception detached. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi, and al-Nasafi give restoration as an alternative; al-Nasafi pictures mercy as its guardian. Al-Zamakhshari includes mercy among protectors, and al-Bursevi prefers mercy personified as its advocate. Al-Alusi reports this connected reading and objects that it strains advocate."}, {"id": "17:87/q02/p3", "position": "It gives revelation or knowledge to the Prophet in the first place.", "reasons": "Yahya ibn Sallam supplies an implied clause about sending the Qur'an. Al-Jishumi calls both descent and preservation mercy. Al-Tabatabai speaks of receiving and retaining the Spirit. Study Quran pairs the revealing and preserving of the Qur'an."}, {"id": "17:87/q02/p4", "position": "It is the special divine manifestation that sustains the Prophet's existence, perfection, knowledge, and revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani contrasts the mercy of the Merciful with direct manifestation of the divine essence, which would leave neither the Prophet's self nor revelation; majesty can veil knowledge."}]}
{"id": "17:87/q03", "question": "What does 'from your Lord' modify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:87/q03/p1", "position": "It modifies mercy directly, or an omitted adjective describing mercy.", "reasons": "Al-Samin reports both grammatical attachments without choosing between them."}]}
{"id": "17:87/q04", "question": "What is God's great favor upon the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause identifies the gift of revelation and its preservation, the Prophet's rank and promised station, the wider gift of knowledge, or an inward or guidance-centered account; several sources combine these.", "positions": [{"id": "17:87/q04/p1", "position": "It includes granting prophethood and the Qur'an, teaching it, and preserving it.", "reasons": "Yahya ibn Sallam names prophethood and revelation; al-Tabari adds the choice of Muhammad for the message and countless revelations. Al-Kashshaf, al-Razi, Abu Hayyan, al-Baydawi, al-Alusi, and Ibn Ashur treat continued preservation as a favor beyond the original gift. Ibn Atiyya adds protection from polytheists; al-Bursevi adds the Seal of the Prophets. Al-Biqai extends the favor to the community. Kur'an Yolu says revelation is transmitted without alteration. Al-Jishumi says divine favor gives what best serves people's religion, not what they wish for."}, {"id": "17:87/q04/p2", "position": "It is Muhammad's precedence over humanity, final prophethood, and the Praiseworthy Station.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas is cited by al-Wahidi and al-Tabrisi; al-Wahidi al-Wajiz, al-Razi, and al-Alusi also give this account. Ibn Atiyya mentions prophethood and protection from polytheists; al-Bursevi includes final prophethood. Study Quran points to 17:79 and 33:40 for excellence and being the Seal."}, {"id": "17:87/q04/p3", "position": "It grants scholars accessible knowledge and keeps what they learn in memory.", "reasons": "Al-Razi counts access to knowledge and its preservation as two favors; al-Kashshaf urges scholars to thank God for both."}, {"id": "17:87/q04/p4", "position": "Its eternal basis is necessary existence, followed by revelation and divine teaching.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani orders the gifts as existence, then revelation and teaching."}, {"id": "17:87/q04/p5", "position": "It does what most conduces to people's guidance and acceptance and best serves their religion.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi contrasts this with doing what people merely wish for."}]}
{"id": "17:87/q05", "question": "In what sense is the favor great?", "turns_on": "Al-Mawardi distinguishes abundance of favor from the greatness of its significance.", "positions": [{"id": "17:87/q05/p1", "position": "The favor is abundant or beyond comparison in extent.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi gives abundance as one explanation. Al-Biqai stresses its immense scale for the Prophet and community; Elmalili says it exceeds favor given to others."}, {"id": "17:87/q05/p2", "position": "The favor is immense in significance.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi gives importance, rather than amount, as the other explanation."}]}
{"id": "17:87/q06", "question": "Who is addressed by the warning and the favor?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular address chiefly cautions the Prophet with wider application or chiefly targets other questioners; al-Alusi rejects the latter.", "positions": [{"id": "17:87/q06/p1", "position": "The Prophet is addressed directly; the warning also extends to others and their knowledge.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports that most commentators extend the singular warning of verse 86 to everyone or to the Prophet and community while taking the last clause of verse 87 as addressed to the Prophet. Elmalili says the Prophet's grace is singular and enables confident speech."}, {"id": "17:87/q06/p2", "position": "The warning chiefly threatens other people with loss for asking about withheld matters.", "reasons": "Abu Sahl, as reported by al-Alusi, mentions questions about the spirit and Hour. The named transmitters and exact descriptions vary."}, {"id": "17:87/q07/p3", "position": "Trust is lost first, prayer last, and people pray without religion before the Qur'an disappears.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf reports Ibn Masud's sequence of lost religious qualities."}, {"id": "17:87/q07/p4", "position": "Islam fades; the Qur'an is lifted in a night, while the elderly retain the declaration of God's oneness.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi cites a report of Hudhayfa authenticated by al-Hakim; it says no verse remains on earth."}, {"id": "17:87/q07/p5", "position": "After a warning against writing alongside the Qur'an, every Qur'anic letter can vanish overnight while favored people keep the declaration of God's oneness.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi attributes this prophetic warning jointly to Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar; it specifies paper and hearts."}, {"id": "17:87/q07/p6", "position": "The Qur'an and other revealed books are lifted to heaven, leaving no verses or guidance in hearts.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi cites an Abu Hurayra report authenticated by al-Hakim; its scope includes books besides the Qur'an."}, {"id": "17:87/q07/p7", "position": "Gabriel takes the Qur'an away.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi cites this transmission from Ibn Abi Hatim."}]}
{"id": "17:87/q08", "question": "Does the warning predict a real removal, and how does that fit preservation?", "turns_on": "Whether the conditional removal is merely hypothetical, predicts end-time events, or promises preservation for a limited span; al-Alusi explicitly reconciles the latter with removal reports.", "positions": [{"id": "17:87/q08/p1", "position": "Removal is a hypothetical threat; mercy in fact prevents it and secures ongoing preservation.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says the surface sense makes removal hypothetical and avoids any need for a recovery agent; Ibn Ashur calls the exception a qualification and cites 15:9 on guarding the Reminder. {"id": "17:87/q09", "question": "What role does the warning and favor play in this passage?", "turns_on": "The notes variously read the passage as a lesson in gratitude, an emphasis on preservation, a reply to a boast, consolation, restraint on questioning, guidance, or confidence; al-Alusi rejects the consolation and question-restraint readings.", "positions": [{"id": "17:87/q09/p1", "position": "The threat teaches gratitude for revealed and preserved knowledge and cautions against conceit.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur connects it to the Qur'an's preceding description as healing and mercy and extends the caution from the Prophet to scholars. Ibn Ashur says the warning states removal explicitly while implying favor, made clear by the next clause."}, {"id": "17:87/q09/p2", "position": "The exception and following clause emphasize the additional favor of preserving the Qur'an after revealing it.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi prefers the disconnected reading because the connected reading would make favor only the first revelation. Al-Alusi finds this unpersuasive."}, {"id": "17:87/q09/p5", "position": "It discourages people from pressing for withheld knowledge such as the spirit or the Hour.", "reasons": "Abu Sahl, reported by al-Alusi, takes it as a threat to others; al-Alusi finds this unpersuasive."}, {"id": "17:87/q09/p6", "position": "God gives what best guides people rather than whatever they wish to receive.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi says divine favor chooses what most benefits people's religion and acceptance."}, {"id": "17:87/q09/p7", "position": "The Prophet can speak confidently because his Lord's favor to him exceeds that to others.", "reasons": "Elmalili ties this confidence to the incomparable greatness of divine grace."}]}

{"id": "18:7/q01", "question": "How does jaʿalnā govern mā and zīnatan?", "turns_on": "Whether jaʿala means making something into something or creating it, and whether zīna expresses result, purpose or circumstance.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q01/p1", "position": "Jaʿalnā means 'made'; mā and zīnatan are its two objects.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās reports this analysis. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān distinguish it from the 'created' analysis; al-Qurṭubī adopts it. Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī say transformation gives zīna the second-object role."}, {"id": "18:7/q01/p2", "position": "Jaʿalnā means 'created'; mā is its object and zīnatan states the purpose of creation.", "reasons": "Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās calls this a good view. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī make its syntax depend on the creation sense of jaʿala."}, {"id": "18:7/q01/p3", "position": "If jaʿalnā means 'created,' zīnatan can be a circumstantial accusative.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn give this alternative alongside the purpose accusative."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q02", "question": "What does mā ʿalā l-arḍ include as the earth's adornment?", "turns_on": "How general mā is; whether humans belong to what is adorned or to those tested; and whether adornment means all creation, selected attractive goods, or spiritually distinguished people.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q02/p1", "position": "Everything on earth is its adornment.", "reasons": "Mujāhid's inclusive reading is repeated by al-Ṭabarī, al-Māwardī and others. Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī prefer its breadth: creation and design point to the Maker, so even ugly or harmful things may be called adornment. Al-Ālūsī answers objections that everything has some benefit, at least as evidence of the Maker. Al-Wāḥidī lists seas, mountains, plants and water; al-Baghawī includes snakes, scorpions and devils as signs of divine unity."}, {"id": "18:7/q02/p2", "position": "The broad sense embraces earthly animals, plants and minerals, with humans included or the noblest among them.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī classifies earthly kinds as mineral, plant and animal and calls humans the noblest animals. Al-Ṭabrisī also includes inanimate life. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Burṣawī and the Study Quran list these kinds; al-Biqāʿī stresses visual and inward attraction. Al-Ālūsī allows humans as ado

rnment in one respect and tested subjects in another, citing 18:46 against al-Qāḍī's exclusion."}, {"id": "18:7/q02/p3", "position": "It broadly denotes nonrational things on earth, including animals, plants and minerals, while tested humans are excluded.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān calls nonrational mā the apparent sense. Al-Rāzī also reports adding minerals, gold and silver to a plant reading."}, {"id": "18:7/q02/p5", "position": "It denotes attractive worldly goods and useful things such as wealth, clothing, fruit, water and livestock.", "reasons": "Reports vary in their lists: trees, fruits, metals, vessels, animals and livestock in al-Jishumī; blessings, clothes, fruit, greenery and water in Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān; wealth and children in al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Kur'an Yolu. Al-Kashshāf and al-Nasafī stress luxuries pleasing inhabitants. Al-Ālūsī rejects such a list as exhaustive of the general wording."}, {"id": "18:7/q02/p6", "position": "It means people or men, who beautify the earth.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī, Mujāhid and reports through Saʿīd ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās give this reading; al-Rāzī notes people as the noblest earthly animal. Ibn al-Anbārī says mā stands for man on this reading. Al-Ālūsī finds a solely rational referent unlikely and suggests people can exemplify the whole."}, {"id": "18:7/q02/p7", "position": "The earth's adornment is its prophets, scholars, saints or devout worshippers.", "reasons": "Al-Qāsim, Sahl and others identify spiritual people; al-Qushayrī says their value is perceived by insight, compares inhabitants' value to their home, and calls God's friends a source of safety. Some versions include caliphs and rulers."}, {"id": "18:7/q02/p8", "position": "It means rulers, caliphs, scholars and commanders.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima's report from Ibn ʿAbbās varies between caliphs, scholars and rulers or rulers, scholars and commanders; Ibn al-Anbārī makes mā stand for man on this personal reading."}, {"id": "18:7/q02/p9", "position": "It is earthly desire and the things made attractive to human nature, including the body's powers and pleasures.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī calls it desires appealing to inhabitants; al-Qāshānī includes the body's self, perception and powers; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī includes goods, children and status. These become attachments and a test."}, {"id": "18:7/q02/p10", "position": "It is what appears yellow in sunlight on earth.", "reasons": "Al-Awzāʿī supplies this visual gloss."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q03", "question": "To whom does lahā assign the adornment?", "turns_on": "Whether lahā identifies the adorned earth or includes its inhabitants, and how its lām attaches syntactically.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q03/p1", "position": "It assigns adornment to the earth itself.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares stars adorning the sky; al-Sāmarrāʾī compares flowers and growth to the adornment of the sky in 15:16 and 37:6, and cites 27:60."}, {"id": "18:7/q03/p2", "position": "It is adornment for the earth and its inhabitants.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī and al-Burṣawī explicitly include inhabitants; Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Zamakhsharī's formulation."}, {"id": "18:7/q03/p3", "position": "The first lām can express the purpose of zīna, be extra, or modify an omitted adjective describing zīna.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn lists the three syntactic possibilities; al-Ālūsī allows attachment to zīna or a description of it."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q04", "question": "What does the lām of linabluwahum attach to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q04/p1", "position": "It attaches to jaʿalnā whether that verb means 'created' or 'made.'", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives the attachment under both senses; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī also attach the testing lām to jaʿalnā."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q05", "question": "To whom do the pronouns in linabluwahum and ayyuhum refer?", "turns_on": "Whether mā itself denotes people or the tested inhabitants must be supplied from context.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q05/p1", "position": "They refer to the earth's inhabitants understood from context.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbārī says the observers are intended if mā denotes plants. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn infer inhabitants from the context; al-Samīn also reports exegetical identifications as shepherds or scholars, righteous people and caliphs."}, {"id": "18:7/q05/p2", "position": "They return to mā when it means a collective of rational beings.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbārī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī allow this on the human reading of mā."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q06", "question": "How does God test people through earthly adornment?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis falls on manifest deeds under commands, disciplined use of benefits, grateful reflection, or response to spiritually distinguished people.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q06/p1", "position": "Adornment is the setting for moral responsibility; commands and prohibitions reveal obedience or disobedience for fitting recompense.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says the trial is intelligible to creatures. Ibn Isḥāq and al-Ṭabrisī stress obedience; al-Jishumī says known deeds become manifest. Al-Biqāʿī contrasts sincere service and pleasure pursued in defiance. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says attractive attachments draw souls into earthly life before judgment. Al-Elmalılı emphasizes reward and punishment."}, {"id": "18:7/q06/p2", "position": "Attractive benefits test whether people master desire, avoid prohibited use, and use lawful goods gratefully and rightly.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim says prohibited desire invites punishment or reward and permissible goods require gratitude and proper spending. ʿUmar prayed for help spending adornment rightly. Al-Ālūsī combines lawful use, thanks and reflection. Asad sees moral character in attitudes to material benefits; Iṣlāḥī contrasts reason directed to the Hereafter with desire for this world."}, {"id": "18:7/q06/p3", "position": "The trial distinguishes gratitude from unbelief and reflection and faith from rejection.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says blessings distinguish the grateful although God knows outcomes. Al-Qurṭubī connects reflection and belief to recompense at resurrection. Al-Biqāʿī says worldly desire conceals the call to infer the Creator's knowledge and power."}, {"id": "18:7/q06/p4", "position": "The adornment tests people's response to prophets and scholars who themselves adorn the earth.", "reasons": "Al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad says the test is which recipients or imitators respond and accept best."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q07", "question": "Does God's testing mean He acquires knowledge of people's deeds?", "turns_on": "Whether divine foreknowledge is compatible with a real human test and alternate human action.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q07/p1", "position": "No; God already knows, and testing manifests deeds or treats people as an examiner would for just recompense.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā, al-Jishumī and al-Qāḍī say the outcomes are known beforehand. The majority reported by al-Rāzī affirm eternal knowledge of particulars; al-Ālūsī adds universals and rejects Hishām's contrary view. Ibn al-Jawzī describes God's dealing with creation as one who tests. Al-Ālūsī says reward then fits each person."}, {"id": "18:7/q07/p2", "position": "Yes; God learns events as they occur, since foreknown outcomes would prevent alternate action and make testing unreal.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam's argument. The majority and al-Ālūsī reject it on the ground of God's eternal knowledge."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q08", "question": "Does the purpose lām mean God's acts are directed toward ends?", "turns_on": "Whether a stated purpose implies a need or intermediary incompatible with divine power.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q08/p1", "position": "Yes; the lām of testing supports purposive divine action.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports the Muʿtazilite appeal to the purpose-connoting lām."}, {"id": "18:7/q08/p2", "position": "No; divine acts cannot be caused by purposes.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī's school argues that requiring an intermediary to attain a purpose would imply divine incapacity."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q09", "question": "What does the test imply about human action and God's will?", "turns_on": "Whether meaningful testing entails human origination of deeds and how that relates to divine control of faith.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q09/p1", "position": "Human deeds originate with people, and God wills good action; otherwise testing and accountability would fail.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī use the verse against compulsion or determinism; Kur'an Yolu adds human will and moral discernment. Al-Qāḍī says duties were imposed for obedience, opposing the claim that some were created for Hell."}, {"id": "18:7/q09/p2", "position": "God alone places faith in hearts.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī puts this alongside the attractiveness of earthly animals, minerals and plants."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q10", "question": "What counts as the best deed in the test?", "turns_on": "Whether excellence is measured chiefly by detachment, obedient and lawful use, inward intention, intellectual restraint, reflection, or a specific spiritual discipline.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q10/p1", "position": "Renouncing worldly attachment and leaving its adornment without being deceived by it.", "reasons": "Abū ʿĀṣim, al-Ḥasan, al-Thawrī, Ibn ʿAṭāʾ and others variously stress

 abandoning adornment, detachment and resisting illusion; Tustarī adds humility, stillness, trust and turning to God. Al-Qurṭubī's asceticism reports refine its inward sense. Al-Ālūsī includes lawful use and reflection. The Study Quran reports al-Ghazzālī on detachment."}, {"id": "18:7/q10/p2", "position": "Following God's commands and doing the most obedient work.", "reasons": "Ibn Isḥāq defines it as following command; al-Ṭabrisī stresses productive obedience; al-Kalbī and others give obedience directly. Al-Jishumī says deeds become manifest for recompense."}, {"id": "18:7/q10/p3", "position": "Using one's allotted worldly goods lawfully and well, with faith, duties, restraint and voluntary good works.", "reasons": "Muqātil stresses wealth's best use. Ibn ʿAṭiyya's father specifies taking one's due, spending rightly, faith, obligations, avoiding prohibitions and recommended acts; al-Qurṭubī praises this and cites 'believe in God and remain upright.' Al-Bayḍāwī adds contentment. Al-Ālūsī combines renunciation, lawful use, gratitude and reflection."}, {"id": "18:7/q10/p4", "position": "Showing the greatest trust and reliance on God amid worldly adornment.", "reasons": "Sahl gives this reading through al-Sulamī, al-Māwardī and Abū Ḥayyān; Tustarī lists trust among the qualities of withdrawal."}, {"id": "18:7/q10/p5", "position": "Having a pure heart, true intention, clear insight and rightly guided conduct.", "reasons": "Fāris stresses truth, purpose and intention; al-Qāsim stresses an empty heart, keen perception and guided comportment. Al-Qushayrī stresses intention and inward purity; al-Māwardī and Abū Ḥayyān report purity and conduct."}, {"id": "18:7/q10/p6", "position": "Possessing sound or complete intellect, avoiding God's prohibitions, and hastening to obedience.", "reasons": "A report attributed to the Prophet gives the three traits; Qatāda singles out complete intellect. Al-Ālūsī says the Prophetic answer is best; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites the same report through al-Durr."}, {"id": "18:7/q10/p7", "position": "Avoiding what is forbidden among worldly adornments.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this criterion; Abū Muslim says resisting prohibited desire earns reward and indulging it punishment."}, {"id": "18:7/q10/p8", "position": "Learning the most from worldly adornment as a sign of its Maker.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī gives the criterion; al-Biqāʿī says desire hides the invitation to infer divine knowledge and power; al-Ālūsī makes worldly beauty a mirror for divine majesty and beauty."}, {"id": "18:7/q10/p9", "position": "Remaining steadfast on the Sunnah.", "reasons": "Sahl gives this measure in al-Sulamī, and al-Jishumī reports it as another definition."}, {"id": "18:7/q10/p10", "position": "Counting one's own deed small and deficient before God's due, rather than relying on its reward.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī reports reward expectation as one measure but prefers the higher standard of minimizing one's act, supported by a cited poem. Al-Sulamī reports forgetting self and deed, annihilation in the Real, and refraining from adorning oneself with deeds."}, {"id": "18:7/q10/p11", "position": "Doing the deed while expecting and counting on its reward.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī reports this measure, then ranks awareness of one's deed's deficiency still higher."}, {"id": "18:7/q10/p12", "position": "Affirming servanthood in both speech and action.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ gives this definition."}, {"id": "18:7/q10/p13", "position": "Engaging worldly adornment without becoming preoccupied by it.", "reasons": "Al-Junayd gives this inward reading."}, {"id": "18:7/q10/p14", "position": "Revering God's knowers and lovers, who adorn the earth.", "reasons": "An anonymous inward reading reported by al-Ālūsī combines their status as adornment with the proper response to them."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q11", "question": "What constitutes asceticism toward the world?", "turns_on": "Whether renunciation is brevity of hopes, an inward preference, outward withdrawal, freedom from praise, or readiness for death.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q11/p1", "position": "Short hopes and contentment with sufficient provision.", "reasons": "Sufyān al-Thawrī says it need not mean rough food or clothing; al-Qurṭubī says short hopes foster sufficiency. Al-Ālūsī ranks contentment with a traveler's provision highest."}, {"id": "18:7/q11/p2", "position": "Renunciation in the heart, so leaving the world is dearer than acquiring it.", "reasons": "Ibrāhīm ibn Adham requires preference for leaving; Ibn al-Mubārak locates renunciation inwardly."}, {"id": "18:7/q11/p3", "position": "Abandoning the whole world whether one likes doing so or not.", "reasons": "Al-Fuḍayl gives this criterion."}, {"id": "18:7/q11/p4", "position": "Disliking praise and commendation.", "reasons": "Al-Awzāʿī defines renunciation this way."}, {"id": "18:7/q11/p5", "position": "Avoiding association with people.", "reasons": "Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith equates love of the world with love of meeting people; al-Fuḍayl calls withdrawal a sign."}, {"id": "18:7/q11/p6", "position": "Loving death.", "reasons": "An unnamed group gives this definition; al-Qurṭubī says short hopes encompasses it."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q12", "question": "How is the interrogative ayyuhum parsed after linabluwahum?", "turns_on": "Whether ayy is an interrogative opening a suspended question or a relative pronoun with an omitted relative-clause subject.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q12/p1", "position": "Ayyuhum is an interrogative nominative subject, aḥsanu its predicate, and the whole question is suspended as the testing verb's object.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says the question retains initial position. Al-Jishumī cites 18:12: an interrogative is not governed by preceding material. Al-Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī explain that testing evokes knowing, asking or consideration. Al-Burṣawī adds ʿamalan as specification."}, {"id": "18:7/q12/p2", "position": "Ayyuhum is a relative pronoun meaning 'the one who'; aḥsanu predicates an omitted huwa, and the relative phrase substitutes for the tested object.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports Sībawayh's analysis. Al-Samīn says its nominative can be built on ḍamma when the relative clause's head is omitted, citing 19:69, or inflected, as an anomalous Maryam reading shows; a poem about greeting the best of Banū Mālik attests nominative ayyuhum. Al-Ālūsī notes that Sībawayh permits rather than requires building and finds the point difficult."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q13", "question": "Why say 'best' when the trial includes bad deeds?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q13/p1", "position": "Excellence is the primary aim, so 'best' is apt even though the trial also discloses bad deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī makes the aim of revealing the excellent decisive."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q14", "question": "Is aḥsanu a true comparative?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q14/p1", "position": "Yes; the comparison is omitted: better than people whose deeds are less good.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī supplies the implicit comparison."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q15", "question": "What follows from knowing God personally manages affairs?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q15/p1", "position": "The wise see their true condition, disdain the world, become content and turn away from it.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī al-Rūdhbārī links this response to knowledge of God's personal governance of affairs."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q16", "question": "How does this verse relate to the removal of adornment in 18:8?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q16/p1", "position": "The next verse shows that earthly beauty is temporary: God will strip it away and leave barren ground.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī cites 18:8. Al-Ṭabrisī glosses ṣaʿīd as earth's surface or a plantless road and juruz as barren, consuming plants; al-Jishumī adds soil or level ground. Al-Ṭabrisī cites Arabic jaraz/ajrāz, al-jazar for a drought year, and a rajaz line. Ibn Kathīr contrasts transience with permanent abode; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says attachments are removed before judgment."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q17", "question": "How does the verse console or guide the Prophet amid rejection?", "turns_on": "Whether the consolation is framed around the audience's trial or the Prophet's inward response to rejection.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q17/p1", "position": "Worldly attractiveness is a test, so rejection by some does not show a failure of his message and he should continue calling them.", "reasons": "Al-Qāḍī in al-Rāzī compares God's continued provision for disbelievers with Muḥammad's continued preaching. Al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī and Abū Ḥayyān say some will believe and some refuse. Iṣlāḥī says unbelief is neither a defect in the Book nor a shortcoming in preaching; Asad links refusal to worldly pride, citing 16:22."}, {"id": "18:7/q17/p2", "position": "The Prophet's grief led him to blame his own spiritual state, and the verse consoles that compassionate self-scrutiny.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says he sought to subdue the self from compassion and reverence when people rejected the Qur'an."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q18", "question": "How does 18:7 connect to other passages of al-Kahf or other verses?", "turns_on": "Which later narrative or verse brings the earlier claim about earthly adornment into view.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q18/p1", "position": "The cave sleepers mirror humanity's awakening from a long seeming day of absorption in worldly adornment.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī invokes 23:114 and 46:35 for the short seeming duration."}, {"id": "18:7/q18/p2", "position": "The command to recite after the cave story resumes the earlier argument about earthly adornment.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī connects 18:27 to the earlier statement, followed by unchanged divine words and absence of refuge."}, {"id": "18:7/q18/p3", "position": "God's enduring reality makes Him better in reward and outcome than vanishing worldly adornment.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī connects

18:42–44 to 18:7–8: people need something to rely on, and their Lord endures."}, {"id": "18:7/q18/p4", "position": "The verse's themes are also discussed under 11:7.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī points readers to four earlier views there without detailing them in this note."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q19", "question": "What reports illustrate the lure of the earth and the worth of deeds?", "turns_on": "The reports illustrate different outcomes or tests: temptation, afterlife reward, refused faith, greed, neglected alms and the state of creation.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q19/p1", "position": "The world is green or lush and sweet; God makes people successors in it to test their action and warns against worldly temptation, especially women.", "reasons": "Qatāda and Abū Saʿīd transmit versions of the Prophetic report; Ibn Kathīr adds that women's temptation first tested Israel. Al-Qurṭubī notes two Abū Saʿīd reports in Muslim about the dangers of worldly blossoms and blessings."}, {"id": "18:7/q19/p2", "position": "Paradise's people would not return for all earthly goods, except a martyr who would return to be killed again for the honor seen.", "reasons": "The reports vary: some say the martyr would return and be killed ten times; others speak of the righteous dead generally. Ibn Ḥibbān and Muslim frame the report as the greater worth of reward than all earthly possessions."}, {"id": "18:7/q19/p3", "position": "A person in Hell would offer everything on earth as ransom despite having refused the lesser pledge not to associate partners with God.", "reasons": "The Musnad report sets all earthly wealth against a refused demand of faith."}, {"id": "18:7/q19/p4", "position": "Greedy accumulation is insatiable and dangerous, while sufficient provision and contentment bring success.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports the Prophet's comparison with a person who eats without becoming full."}, {"id": "18:7/q19/p5", "position": "Livestock owners who die without paying zakat leave an obligation unmet.", "reasons": "Muslim's report names camels, cattle and sheep as earthly wealth subject to conduct."}, {"id": "18:7/q19/p6", "position": "The Creator can make harmful animals harmless and visibly beautiful in an age of universal obedience.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says children will play with them in Jesus's time."}]}
{"id": "18:7/q20", "question": "How does earthly adornment serve al-Kahf's larger argument?", "turns_on": "Whether the sūra's frame is its parables generally or its Makkan conflict and exhortation.", "positions": [{"id": "18:7/q20/p1", "position": "The sūra's parables contrast faith with undue attachment to worldly life, especially the story of the rich and poor men.", "reasons": "Asad calls earthly beauty as test the sūra's central idea."}, {"id": "18:7/q20/p2", "position": "The passage addresses late Makkan conflict: Quraysh's worldly success blinds them, while the Prophet and companions should persevere.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī situates al-Kahf after a sūra exposing Jews and alongside Maryam exposing Christians; Quraysh, indirectly backed by Jews and Christians, risk rejecting clear truth and punishment. He also sees hints of migration and victories. Worldly pleasure and status are immediate, while pains are hidden and the Hereafter unseen, making reason and patience essential."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q01", "question": "How does the making construction work?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q01/p1", "position": "Jaʿl denotes transformation, with ṣaʿīdan as its second object and a future sense in the active participle.", "reasons": "Jishumī calls ṣaʿīdan accusative as the object of jāʿilūn; al-Samīn specifies the second object because this use of jaʿala means making one thing into another. Al-Ālūsī also takes jaʿl as transformation. Ibn ʿĀshūr says jāʿilūn is an active participle referring to the future. Al-Burhān discusses other examples where the source and result of transformation are explicit and notes two possible analyses of maʿāsh in 'day a livelihood.'"}]}
{"id": "18:8/q02", "question": "What does 'what is on it' include?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase ranges over all earthly contents or specifically resumes the adornment of 18:7.", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q02/p1", "position": "Everything placed on earth, including living beings and other contents.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says this extends more broadly than the preceding adornment and that repeating the full phrase in place of a pronoun intensifies it; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī suggests the repetition stresses that the adornment is upon earth. Ibn Isḥāq and Ibn ʿAbbās speak of all that is on earth perishing; al-Biqāʿī extends the affliction from vegetation to human and other animals. The Study Quran reports al-Rāzī's view that humanity is the noblest of earth's creatures."}, {"id": "18:8/q02/p2", "position": "The adornment or attractive things on earth mentioned in the preceding verse.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān explicitly allows what adorned earth as the referent. Al-Samarrāʾī says the ornament belongs to earth and its growth, especially flowers that delight the viewer, comparing God's adornment of the sky in 15:16 and 37:6 and earthly beauty in 27:60. The Study Quran lists plants, animals, gold and metals; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī includes goods, children and status as worldly attractions."}]}
